lines.text: January seventh, nineteen forty-eight. Captain Thomas Mantell, twenty-five years old, a decorated war hero, climbs into a fighter plane to chase something in the sky. Within the hour, he is dead.
The newspapers said he died chasing a flying saucer. It was the first time anyone had lost their life, so it seemed, to a UFO.
So tonight, we climb. We follow the flight rung by rung, from the ground to the last altitude he ever reached. Every claim gets checked against the record.
At each height, we ask what is evidence, and what is rumor. Then we look at the suspects: a planet, a reflection, a secret balloon, and a spaceship.
At the end, a verdict. Let's start on the ground, at one fifteen in the afternoon.

One fifteen in the afternoon. In the control tower at Godman Field, beside Fort Knox, Kentucky, the phone rings. It is the state highway patrol. People near Maysville are reporting a strange aircraft.
Godman checks with flight service at Wright Field in Ohio. No traffic. About twenty minutes later, the police call again. Now it is Owensboro and Irvington, far to the west.
Those towns describe something circular, about two hundred and fifty to three hundred feet across, moving west at, quote, a pretty good clip. The report is passed to Fort Knox.
At one forty-five, the tower sees it too. The assistant operator watches it for several minutes before he says a word. He does not want to, quote, make a flying saucer report.
The chief is called. Then the operations officer. Then the intelligence officer. Then the base commander, Colonel Guy Hix. Each looks through the tower's big binoculars. Nobody can name it.
They say it is not an airplane. They say it is not a weather balloon. One calls it a parachute. Another says an ice cream cone tipped with red.
Others say round and white. Huge and silver. One fourth the size of the full moon. A small white thing. The descriptions disagree. But almost all of them describe something big.
Around two thirty, four fighter planes come into view from the south. The National Guard, flying home from Georgia. The tower calls the leader, Captain Mantell.
Mantell is twenty-five. In the war, he flew a transport plane on D-Day and towed gliders under heavy fire. He earned the Distinguished Flying Cross. He has a wife, Peggy, and two small sons.
One of the four is low on fuel and flies on home. Mantell takes his two wingmen, turns, and heads toward the object. The tower directs them. At first, none of the pilots can even see it.
They climb. The fighter is a North American F-51, the same plane the world knows as the P-51 Mustang. It is fast, and it is powerful, but it is built for low and middle altitude.
By ten thousand feet, the two wingmen see Mantell pulling away. He is ahead, climbing hard, and just barely in sight.
Then, around two forty-five, his voice on the radio. Quote, I see something above and ahead of me, and I'm still climbing. Everyone in the tower hears it.
One of the wingmen answers with a question that survives in the record. What the hell are we looking for? They cannot see a thing.
The tower asks Mantell for a description. And here the story starts to bend. Nobody in the tower can later remember his exact words. And, despite the rumors, there is no recording.
Saucer writers later credited him with a famous line. Quote, it looks metallic, and it's tremendous in size. The line was repeated everywhere. But the tower never agreed he said it.
What the tower did hear, all of them, was the last clear sentence. Quote, I'm going to twenty thousand feet.
Now the rule that matters most. Every pilot in those days was taught the same thing. Do not go above fifteen thousand feet without oxygen.

Captain Edward Ruppelt, who later ran the Air Force's UFO project, took the training himself, in a pressure chamber. A few tough men reached fifteen thousand feet without a mask. Nobody got past seventeen.
Lack of oxygen is called hypoxia. It is quiet. First you feel fine, even happy. Then your judgment goes. Then your vision. Then you black out, and you never notice it coming.
The wingmen carry no oxygen either. At fifteen thousand feet, they stop. They call Mantell. No answer. They start to come back down.
One of them says something on the way home. All he had seen, he says, was a reflection on his canopy. We will come back to that.
Mantell goes on alone. Fifteen thousand. Sixteen. Eighteen. Twenty. He is chasing something above him that, as he flies, seems to climb away.
Back at Godman, the radio goes quiet. Calls to Mantell get no answer. He will never speak to anyone again.

Why would a careful pilot do it? A friend who flew with him for years said Mantell was one of the most cautious men he knew. His guess was that he was after something he believed more important than his life.
Or maybe the plan was simple. Climb fast to twenty thousand, take a look, drop back down before the oxygen runs out. In a fighter this strong, it might have felt safe. It was a bet he could not win.
Investigators later reconstructed it from the wreck. The throttle setting, the debris, the way the plane fell. Somewhere near twenty-five thousand feet, Mantell passed out.
With a hand off the controls, the plane kept climbing for a while, up to around thirty thousand feet, before it fell off and started to turn.
Then came the spiral. Witnesses on the ground saw it circling down. The speed built and built.
Near Franklin, Kentucky, on a farm, about four miles southwest of town, the fighter hit the ground. Mantell's watch had stopped at three eighteen.
The accident report is plain. The plane had lost a wing in a dive, from too much speed, after the pilot blacked out from lack of oxygen.
His seat belt was shredded. Word reached the tower within minutes. It was a terrible, ordinary crash.
A young man was dead. A wife lost her husband. Two boys lost their father. And by dark, the newspapers had a headline.
Quote, F-51 and Captain Mantell destroyed chasing flying saucer. The Louisville Courier printed it that same day. Not a theory. A headline.
What happened next is a lesson in how a rumor grows. Within days, the crash was a legend.
The rumors said a spacecraft shot him down. That a ray hit him. That small holes were found in the plane.
They said his body was riddled with bullets. They said it was missing. That the plane came apart in mid-air. That the wreck was radioactive. Historian Curtis Peebles collected them all.
Ruppelt wired for the real accident report. His summary is short. The body was not burned. It was not disintegrated. It was not full of holes.
The wreck was not radioactive. It was not magnetized. A wing was gone because the plane dived too fast. There was no ray, and no gunfire.
So the crash itself is explained. The mystery is the other question. What was he chasing? Three suspects. We start with the cheapest.
Time for the first suspect: a planet, and a reflection.
Suspect one: Venus. Project Sign, the Air Force's first UFO study, said so almost before the rescue crews reached the crash.
There was a reason. Weeks earlier, a fighter pilot had chased Venus. And at three o'clock that afternoon, Venus was in the southwest, in nearly the right place, at about thirty-three degrees high.
The tower guessed forty-five degrees. Close enough, with human error. But there was a problem. Venus was only about six times brighter than the daytime sky. Almost impossible to see.
The astronomer J. Allen Hynek did the math himself. He had helped write the Venus answer. Then he took it back. Venus, he told Ruppelt, was not bright enough, and the day was hazy.
That evening, at seven twenty, about a dozen towers did report a light low in the southwest. The Air Force says that one was Venus. Fine. But that was hours after Mantell.
Suspect one and a half: a reflection on the canopy. A wingman said it, as he flew home. But Ruppelt asked a dozen pilots. A canopy flare fools you for a second or two.

Mantell chased his object for something like fifteen to twenty minutes, while it was seen from the ground, with binoculars, at the same time. A reflection does not do that. A sundog has fuzzy edges and fades when you climb.
So Venus is out as a full explanation, and the canopy and the sundog too. That leaves a stranger answer, and a secret.
Suspect two: a Skyhook balloon. In nineteen forty-eight, the Navy and the Air Force were launching enormous research balloons. One hundred feet across, and rising to sixty thousand feet or higher.

They were highly classified. Mantell had never heard of one. The men in the tower had not either. Seen from far away, in low winter sun, it would look like a parachute, or an ice cream cone with a red tip.

In nineteen fifty-two, Ruppelt had the winds reconstructed. A balloon launched from Clinton County in Ohio could drift west, be seen at Maysville, then Owensboro, then slide south past Godman, at the height Mantell could never reach.

And buried in the file were two forgotten reports. A man at Madisonville, looking through a telescope: a balloon. And an astronomer near Nashville that afternoon: a balloon, pear-shaped, with cables and a basket.
But here is the gap. Nobody has ever found a launch record for January seventh. Ruppelt looked. Veterans remembered flying from Clinton County. They would not be pinned to that day.
Critics add a second problem. That Nashville balloon was perhaps a hundred and fifty miles away. The balloon fits the descriptions very well. It does not, however, come with a paper trail.
Debrief. Time to score the Mantell case.
A real chase and a real crash: evidence. Many witnesses on the ground saw a large object: evidence. Mantell died from lack of oxygen: evidence, from the accident report. Venus alone: unlikely.
A Skyhook balloon: the best fit, but still unproven. A ray, bullets, or a shoot-down: debunked. A spacecraft: no evidence at all.
The verdict. Case closed on the death. Open on the object, but narrowing. Mantell died of hypoxia, chasing what was most likely a secret balloon he had no way of knowing about.
The saddest part is that nothing alien is needed. A brave pilot, in a hurry to see something no one could name, went one rung too high. We still remember him by the thing he chased.
Next case: that same year, over Fargo, a young pilot, a light that danced, and a dogfight that nobody could explain. Was it real?
What do you think Mantell saw? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next ancient mystery put to the test.
